Stage 02

Statutory Formation & Board Resolutions

Competent registry, governing statute, capital lockup rules, and first board resolution template.

Competent corporate registry

Registro Mercantil Central (Central Commercial Registry) for the name certificate and Registro Mercantil Provincial (Provincial Commercial Registry) for the final registration of the deed, both overseen by the Ministry of Justice (Ministerio de Justicia).

Governing statute

Real Decreto Legislativo 1/2010, de 2 de julio, by which the consolidated text of the Ley de Sociedades de Capital (Spanish Capital Companies Act) is approved; applicable formation and capital sections are Articles 20-32 (formation), 58-61 (registered office), 62-65 (share capital), and 100-104 (administration and officer appointment).

Formation / constitutional filings

Escritura de Constitución (public deed of incorporation) and its mandatory inscription in the Registro Mercantil Provincial.

Incorporation processing time

⚡ 35 business days (SOP sum)

Paid-up Capital & Blocked Account Regime No Capital Lockup Account Required

The SL must have a minimum subscribed and fully paid-up share capital of EUR 3,000. The capital must be deposited in a Spanish bank account in the Company's name before execution of the deed; the bank's Certificado de Desembolso (capital deposit certificate) must be presented to the notary. The deposited capital cannot be withdrawn until the Company is registered in the Commercial Registry. Non-cash contributions require an independent valuation report under Article 67 LSC.

Funding & unlock path: Fire protection certificate (Certificado de Instalación y Mantenimiento de Protección Contra Incendios), building occupancy and structural inspection certificate (ITEO/ITE) issued by a certified architect, and workplace health and safety verification (Plan de Prevención de Riesgos Laborales) notified to the competent labor authority through the applicable mutua.

Paid-in capital rule: The SL must have a minimum subscribed and fully paid-up share capital of EUR 3,000. The capital must be deposited in a Spanish bank account in the Company's name before execution of the deed; the bank's Certificado de Desembolso (capital deposit certificate) must be presented to the notary. The deposited capital cannot be withdrawn until the Company is registered in the Commercial Registry. Non-cash contributions require an independent valuation report under Article 67 LSC.

Pro-Forma First Board Resolution Draft
RESOLVED THAT the incorporation deed and Bylaws of the Company be approved and that the directors be authorized to execute and file all constitutional instruments. RESOLVED THAT the statutory share capital of EUR 3,000 has been fully subscribed and paid up by the founding members as set forth in the bank certificate. RESOLVED THAT the registered office of the Company be fixed at Calle de la Industria 45, Madrid, Spain, within jurisdiction of the Madrid Commercial Registry. RESOLVED THAT the Company's Executive Chair and Secretary be appointed, and that the Managing Director be granted daily authority to open bank accounts, obtain tax registration, engage employees, and complete municipal licensing. All resolutions effective upon registration.
Industrial Access / EIA & Civil Defense Approval Exempted / Not Required

Dirección General de Industria, Energía y Minas de la Comunidad de Madrid and Concejalía de Urbanismo, Medio Ambiente y Movilidad del Ayuntamiento de Madrid.

Stage 03

Tax Identity & Indirect Tax

Tax authority e-portal, entity tax classification elections, VAT thresholds, and 0% export documentation chain.

Tax ID Application Infrastructure

Competent tax authority

Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT), through its Sede Electrónica (Electronic Office). Regional tax authorities administer certain taxes in the Basque Country and Navarre; the target jurisdiction is otherwise subject to the common national tax regime.

E-government filing portal

A Spanish SL obtains a Spanish NIF through the AEAT. Following incorporation, its representative files Modelo 036 to obtain or confirm the NIF, ordinarily using the incorporation deed and evidence of registration or pending registration with the Commercial Registry. A provisional NIF may be issued during formation; the definitive NIF must be confirmed after registration and completion of the required filings. A foreign legal entity conducting taxable activity in Spain applies for a Spanish NIF using Modelo 036 and supplies formation, registry, identity, and representative documentation, with legalization or translation where required. For VAT transactions requiring an EU VAT number, the entity requests inclusion in the Registro de Operadores Intracomunitarios (ROI) through Modelo 036; the resulting VAT number is validated through VIES. A non-EU taxable person may be required to appoint a Spanish VAT fiscal representative, subject to applicable EU rules and exemptions. Tax registration does not itself establish a permanent establishment or determine corporate tax residence.

Tax ID type & application path: Entity_Level_Taxation — A Spanish SL obtains a Spanish NIF through the AEAT. Following incorporation, its representative files Modelo 036 to obtain or confirm the NIF, ordinarily using the incorporation deed and evidence of registration or pending registration with the Commercial Registry. A provisional NIF may be issued during formation; the definitive NIF must be confirmed after registration and completion of the required filings. A foreign legal entity conducting taxable activity in Spain applies for a Spanish NIF using Modelo 036 and supplies formation, registry, identity, and representative documentation, with legalization or translation where required. For VAT transactions requiring an EU VAT number, the entity requests inclusion in the Registro de Operadores Intracomunitarios (ROI) through Modelo 036; the resulting VAT number is validated through VIES. A non-EU taxable person may be required to appoint a Spanish VAT fiscal representative, subject to applicable EU rules and exemptions. Tax registration does not itself establish a permanent establishment or determine corporate tax residence.

Default Tax Classification & Elections

Default tax classification

Entity_Level_Taxation

Available election forms

A Spanish SL is generally a separate corporate income-tax taxpayer; Spain has no general US-style check-the-box election for an SL. Statutory optional regimes may be available subject to eligibility and election requirements, including tax consolidation and specified special regimes. Hybrid-mismatch rules apply under Spanish law and EU-derived provisions; they do not constitute a general entity-classification election.

VAT / GST & 0% Export Zero-Rating

Standard VAT / GST rate

21%

Mandatory registration threshold (Nexus)

No general domestic turnover threshold: a taxable person carrying out VAT-taxable activity in mainland Spain or the Balearic Islands generally must register before commencing the activity. The EU-wide EUR 10,000 threshold applies only to specified cross-border intra-EU distance sales and qualifying electronically supplied or other telecommunications, broadcasting, and electronic services under the applicable rules; it is not a general Spanish domestic registration threshold. The Canary Islands, Ceuta, and Melilla are outside the EU VAT territory and have separate indirect-tax regimes.

Export 0% zero-rating conditions

Exports of goods dispatched or transported from the EU VAT territory to a destination outside it may qualify for the Spanish VAT export exemption with entitlement to deduct input VAT, provided the statutory exporter, supply, and documentary conditions are met and the export is properly evidenced. The exemption may also apply to qualifying services directly connected with exports or other specifically listed services. Services are not generally zero-rated merely because the customer is located offshore: place-of-supply rules, customer status, use-and-enjoyment provisions, and any applicable exemption must be assessed. Intra-EU supplies are governed by separate exemption conditions and are not exports for this purpose.

  • Commercial invoice identifying the parties, goods, consideration, and applicable VAT treatment
  • Export customs declaration and evidence of exit from the EU customs territory, ordinarily including the MRN and customs exit confirmation
  • Transport evidence appropriate to the route, such as a bill of lading, air waybill, CMR consignment note, or carrier delivery records
  • Sales order, contract, packing list, and proof linking the goods supplied to the export declaration and transport records
  • For services, contract, service-delivery evidence, customer identity and business-status evidence, and documentation supporting the applicable place-of-supply or exemption treatment
  • Inward remittance evidence only where relevant to substantiate payment or commercial records; it is not a universal statutory condition for export VAT exemption

Spain does not generally require advance real-time tax-authority clearance of every domestic VAT invoice. The Immediate Supply of Information system (SII) requires qualifying taxpayers, including those subject to monthly VAT returns and certain electing taxpayers, to electronically report invoice-record data to the AEAT, generally within four days subject to statutory counting rules and exceptions. The Veri*Factu and electronic invoicing requirements under Law 11/2021 and Law 18/2022 are subject to implementing rules and applicable rollout dates; taxpayers must verify the rules effective for their accounting system and transaction date. B2B electronic invoicing under Law 18/2022 is being implemented progressively and is not a universal clearance or digital-stamping regime.

The taxpayer must retain reliable evidence supporting the export exemption and input-tax deduction and produce it during an AEAT audit. If the exemption is unsupported or conditions are not met, the AEAT may assess output VAT, deny or recover input-VAT refunds, charge late-payment interest, and impose penalties under the General Tax Law. Depending on the facts and severity, tax penalties can generally range from 50% to 150% of the unpaid tax; separate penalties may apply for accounting, invoicing, or reporting violations. Fraudulent conduct may also trigger criminal liability where statutory thresholds and elements are met.

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

Spain operates a fully liberalised and freely convertible currency regime. Both current-account and capital-account transactions are unrestricted under Articles 63–66 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and under Spanish Law 18/1962 (as amended) on the foreign-exchange banking regime. The euro (EUR) is fully convertible, and there are no surrender requirements, no central-bank prior-approval procedures, no soft-exchange-rate controls and no exchange-rationing rules. Profit remittances by an SL (Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada) to non-resident shareholders are freely permitted, but the paying company must satisfy: (i) the distributable-capital safeguards of the Ley de Sociedades de Capital, including the mandatory legal reserve of 5% of annual profit until the reserve reaches 20% of share capital, the set-off of prior-year losses and the absence of a net-asset deficit; (ii) the corporate-income-tax (IS) settlement and the correct accounting base; (iii) the non-resident withholding tax applicable to dividends (the WHT is reduced under double-tax-treaty networks and generally 19% for eligible EU/EEA residents, with the standard statutory rate for other non-residents); and (iv) bank-level reporting of the payment under the Banco de España external-transactions statistics and AML/CFT rules. The practical hurdle is not legal convertibility but documentary proportionality: receiving/remitting banks must evidence the economic substance of flows, the underlying commercial or capital instrument, and the tax status of the beneficiary before executing any significant Latin American or Asian corridor payment. Spain maintains no list of blocked currencies and no priority foreign-exchange allocation scheme; capital exports could only be restricted by an exceptional EU-wide safeguard (e.g., financial-sanctions measures related to sanctioned counterparties), none of which applies to this low-risk micro-mobility manufacturing entity.

Export proceeds surrender rules

No statutory export-proceeds surrender rule, no mandatory conversion timeline and no required conversion ratio apply in Spain. Exporters may invoice, hold, collect and convert export receipts in any convertible currency; there is no obligation to repatriate export proceeds within a fixed period and no obligation to convert USD, MXN, BRL or CNY collections into EUR. The mandatory disciplines for this ISIC 3091 electric cargo e-bike manufacturer are documentary and statistical: (i) extra-EU exports require a customs export declaration (DUA) lodged in the Spanish Customs electronic system, with the export-VAT exemption (0% VAT) evidenced on the commercial invoice; (ii) intra-EU dispatches to other Member States are monitored through the Intrastat threshold (approximately EUR 400,000 annual dispatch threshold for goods) and must be declared to the Spanish Tax Administration (AEAT); (iii) export collections arriving through the banking system must carry the underlying invoice and transport documents so that the receiving bank can classify the flow in the Banco de España external operations statistics; and (iv) the export prices and proceeds must comply with the transfer-pricing arm's-length principle where the buyer is a related party. The practical operational rule is that all export receipts are credited to the SL's domestic EUR-denominated account, optionally after a spot conversion by the bank at the ECB reference rate; the exporter must simply preserve the customs, invoice, banking and transport evidence for inspection by AEAT, the customs authority and the financial institution.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España (Bank of Spain) in coordination with the Dirección General de Comercio Internacional e Inversiones (DGCIIN) of the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Business; the Banco de España is the supervisory authority for credit institutions, payment systems, balance-of-payments statistics and the external-transaction reporting regime, while the DGCIIN administers the Registro de Inversiones Exteriores (foreign investment registry). Spain is a Eurozone member, so monetary policy and foreign-reserve management are ultimately vested in the European Central Bank within the Eurosystem, with the Banco de España acting as the national competent authority.

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Cross-border EMI / Fintech rails Fit: High

Feasibility rating: MEDIUM for EU-licensed Electronic Money Institutions that hold a valid PSD2 passport into Spain; LOW for offshore or non-EU digital EMIs. A Spanish SL may lawfully hold payment accounts with an EU-authorised EMI, but an EMI is not a credit institution, is not supervised by the Banco de España as a bank, cannot grant overdraft or working-capital credit, cannot issue commercial documentary letters of credit or standby guarantees in the manner of a Tier-1 bank, and its deposit-like balances do not benefit from the Fondo de Garantía de Depósitos (Spanish deposit-guarantee scheme); immunity is replaced by the safeguarding/segregation duties of the EMD. Offshore EMIs (e.g., UK post-Brexit, BVI, UAE, Gibraltar-based) are not passportable into Spain without a local licence or authorised agent under the Payment Services Law (RDL 19/2018 transposing PSD2), so their onboarding of a Spanish manufacturing SL is either illegal or operationally crippled by correspondent-bank sanctions screening. For this micro-mobility OEM, which must pay Chinese component suppliers, collect LatAm distributor proceeds, settle Spanish payroll/VAT and ultimately remit dividends, an EMI-only treasury is not viable. The recommended configuration is a Tier-1 Spanish bank as the principal operating account and EBICS-connected gateway, optionally supplemented by one EU-passporting EMI multi-currency wallet for low-value, high-volume supplier float; any non-EU foreign account held by the SL must be disclosed to AEAT on Form 720 before 31 March of the following year, and balances above EUR 50,000 require the annual asset declaration, all of which raises compliance cost.

Core KYC Rejection Triggers & Defense Dossier

Unexplained source of wealth for subscribed capital and initial working capital injected by non-resident shareholders, especially if the parent or ultimate beneficial owner resides in a LATAM high-risk jurisdiction or an Asian manufacturing corridor.

Root cause: Unexplained source of wealth for subscribed capital and initial working capital injected by non-resident shareholders, especially if the parent or ultimate beneficial owner resides in a LATAM high-risk jurisdiction or an Asian manufacturing corridor.

Defense evidence: Notarised Escritura de Aumento de Capital or escritura de constitución, registered at the Registro Mercantil with the new capital inscription; UBO registry certificates from the foreign parent jurisdiction; three months of parent bank statements evidencing lawful accumulation of funds from real operating revenues; certified corporate financial statements and tax returns of the parent for the last two years; a signed source-of-wealth declaration aligned with FATCA/CRS classifications; and a board-approved written explanation of the economic purpose (component procurement, inventory build-up and export expansion for electric cargo e-bikes).
High-frequency supplier payments to Chinese, Vietnamese or Turkish vendors in round-sum amounts that do not match Incoterms, transport documents or customs entries, creating trade-based money-laundering suspicion.

Root cause: High-frequency supplier payments to Chinese, Vietnamese or Turkish vendors in round-sum amounts that do not match Incoterms, transport documents or customs entries, creating trade-based money-laundering suspicion.

Defense evidence: Master supplier framework agreements; foreign trade licences or business-registry excerpts of the vendors; per-shipment commercial invoices and packing lists; Bills of Lading, CMRs or air waybills consistent with the payment value and dates; customs export/import declarations (DUAs) for extra-EU movements or Intrastat declarations for intra-EU flows; HS-code evidence (CN 8507 batteries, CN 8711 e-bike chassis and electric-power groups); inventory serial-number traceability records; and an audit-ready statement confirming that each wire corresponds to physical goods in transit and not to transfer-pricing round-trips or commission laundering.
LatAm distributor proceeds arriving through PSE/acquirer settlement platforms or via third-country financial intermediaries with fragmented FX conversion trails, particularly Mexican Peso, Chilean Peso, Argentine Peso and Brazilian Real receivables.

Root cause: LatAm distributor proceeds arriving through PSE/acquirer settlement platforms or via third-country financial intermediaries with fragmented FX conversion trails, particularly Mexican Peso, Chilean Peso, Argentine Peso and Brazilian Real receivables.

Defense evidence: Executed distributor agreements with resale and exclusivity clauses; the AEAT-matching export declarations and transport evidence proving physical export of goods; FX conversion confirmations issued by the clearing banks or the licensed broker showing ECB/IberEfx reference rates; reconciliation ledgers mapping the acquirer/payment-provider payout reports to specific bank statement credits; Incoterm-based pricing sheets (FOB/CIF/DAP) for each destination; and a statutory declaration certified by the administrator that no informal money brokers, VASPs or shell payment agents were used for the collection chain.
One or more directors, shareholders or beneficial owners being classified as politically exposed persons (PEPs) or persons with a criminal/tax-condemnation record, or the SL's management profile containing a legacy insolvency from another jurisdiction.

Root cause: One or more directors, shareholders or beneficial owners being classified as politically exposed persons (PEPs) or persons with a criminal/tax-condemnation record, or the SL's management profile containing a legacy insolvency from another jurisdiction.

Defense evidence: Individual KYC packet for each administrator: valid DNI/NIE/passport, current proof of residential address (utility bill or tax receipt), Certificado de Antecedentes Penales with legalisation/apostille from Spain or the home jurisdiction, a signed PEP-status questionnaire, and a non-PEP/non-sanctions self-certification; explanation letter covering any adverse historical public-record event and its judicial resolution; and the bank's internal elevated-monitoring acceptance form with the compliance officer's approval where PEP status is unavoidable.
Divergence between the SL's declared tax census activity (IAE epígrafe / NACE code) and the real transaction mix, e.g., the bank observes dividend remittances, intellectual-property royalty payments or large unrelated-party payments inconsistent with a manufacturing entity.

Root cause: Divergence between the SL's declared tax census activity (IAE epígrafe / NACE code) and the real transaction mix, e.g., the bank observes dividend remittances, intellectual-property royalty payments or large unrelated-party payments inconsistent with a manufacturing entity.

Defense evidence: AEAT Censo Certificado (Certificado de Censos) updated to NACE 30.91 / IAE epígrafe 316.1/316.2; the Spanish corporate-income-tax (IS) settlement and net-asset position; a board-approved annual treasury plan listing expected imports, payroll, plant-rents, equipment capex, intra-group service fees and dividend distributions; the Junta General minutes authorising any dividend and demonstrating compliance with the legal reserve requirement; and a transaction-specific narrative for each unusual flow, including the underlying commercial contract and the applicable tax form (e.g., Form 216 for dividend withholding, Form 123/124 or IRNR declarations for interest/royalties).
Potential undisclosed foreign bank accounts or fintech wallets held in offshore EMIs by the Spanish entity or its shareholders, triggering AEAT Form 720 penalties and reputational AML concerns.

Root cause: Potential undisclosed foreign bank accounts or fintech wallets held in offshore EMIs by the Spanish entity or its shareholders, triggering AEAT Form 720 penalties and reputational AML concerns.

Defense evidence: Complete Form 720 'Declaración informativa sobre bienes y derechos situados en el extranjero' filed on time with the AEAT presentation receipt; a written group policy that all non-EU and non-bank payment accounts are individually listed and centrally controlled; the SL's treasury manual containing a defined whitelist of approved EMI accounts and maximum balance thresholds; periodic reconciliations signed by the administrator; and an independent compliance attestation confirming that no undisclosed accounts or crypto-assets are used to receive trade proceeds.

Cross-Border Clearing Corridors & Settlement Fit

Compliant protocol for inbound equity injections, shareholder loans and pre-export working-capital transfers from non-resident parents: (1) Legal perfection: for equity, execute a notarised Escritura de Aumento de Capital and register it at the Registro Mercantil; for shareholder loans, execute a private or notarised loan agreement with commercial-rate interest and file it with the annual financial statements; (2) Wire routing: the foreign parent sends a SWIFT MT103 through its correspondent bank to the SL's Spanish IBAN, which must carry the full Spanish NIF of the SL in the beneficiary field; the sending bank should use an OECD balance-of-payments purpose code equivalent to 'direct investment, equity injection' (e.g., S301/S302 or Banco de España external-transactions concept code for capital contributions, such as the 'Inversión Directa' category of the external statistics regime); (3) Documentation to the destination bank: certified capital-increase deed, bank-supported UBO declaration, Notary date-stamped inscription proof, and the bank's standard 'Justificación de operaciones con el exterior' declaration; (4) Foreign investment registry: direct foreign investments are declared ex-post to the Registro de Inversiones Exteriores (through the form T-01/DGCIIN) within 30 days of the operation or at the latest before the annual filing deadline; no prior exchange-control authorisation is required because the foreign-investment-screening rules only apply to a short list of security-sensitive sectors, not to micro-mobility manufacturing; (5) FX conversion: if the injection is in USD, CNY or a LatAm currency, the receiving bank converts at the ECB reference rate with a transparent spread and issues an exchange confirmation used for accounting and the cash-flow reconciliation; (6) Anti-money-laundering verification: the outgoing corresponding bank must show the SL's legal name, full address, NIF and the purpose reference 'Aportación de capital / Fondo de comercio exterior' on the MT103, and all originator/beneficiary fields must be fully populated to survive travel-rule and sanctions screening; any inbound transfer exceeding EUR 10,000 will be reviewed, and the SL must be prepared to deliver the underlying capital documentation within 48 hours.Clearing-rail matrix for outbound disbursements: (1) EU component suppliers: use SEPA Credit Transfers (SCT) in EUR with purpose code 'Payment for goods' — these are instant to T+1, zero-FX and benefit from the single euro payments framework; the SL should configure SCT mandates and EBICS electronic banking for each recurring vendor; (2) Extra-EU supplier payments (China, Vietnam, Turkey, UK): SWIFT MT103 via the bank's correspondent network with global-payment-innovation (gpi) and a unique end-to-end transaction reference (UETR); each MT103 must include the supplier's full legal name, address, commercial invoice number, customs DUA reference where available, and the goods description in HS-code form; (3) Large component lots: documentary Letters of Credit under UCP600 (sight or 30–90 days) issued via SWIFT MT700 through Santander, BBVA or CaixaBank, with transport documents, packing lists, commercial invoices, certificates of origin and inspection certificates presented in strict conformity; a standby LC (SBLC) may support an advance-payment contract; (4) LatAm customer collections: payments are received primarily as MT103 credits; for Argentine and Venezuelan buyers with inconvertible local currencies, collection is structured through an NDF-based settlement or a confirming house mechanism, never through informal parallel FX brokers; (5) Profit remittances and dividends: outbound MT103 wires from the SL to foreign shareholders with the concept 'Dividend distribution', supported by the Junta General distribution minutes and the Form 216 withholding settlement; the paying bank requires proof of AEAT acceptance before releasing the remittance; (6) Governance: all outbound wires above EUR 10,000 are executed only after a five-eye check in the treasury platform; the SL maintains a sanctioned-party screening database of all suppliers, freight forwarders, insurers and bank counterparts; and the treasury manual requires that the purpose code, invoice number and underlying contract identifier be present on every payment instruction, ensuring full auditability for AEAT, the Banco de España, the customs authority and any future external auditor.Deliverable FX Forwards (EUR/USD, EUR/MXN, EUR/BRL, EUR/CNH) executed with a licensed Spanish credit institution or an EU-regulated broker under MiFID II documentation, used to lock conversion rates for commercial settlements with LatAm distributors and Asian component suppliers.Non-Deliverable Forwards (NDFs) for restricted or low-convertibility currencies (EUR/ARS, EUR/VES) since physical delivery of Argentine and Venezuelan Pesos is prohibited or impractical under the respective local central-bank capital controls; the NDF is settled in EUR against an agreed reference rate and must always be evidenced by underlying commercial receivables or payables.Cross-Currency Swaps (CCS or FX swaps) between EUR and USD/CNH for matching long-lived, capex-denominated import liabilities and for sculpting the maturity profile of shareholder loans, subject to ISDA/CSA documentation and EMIR clearing-margin obligations where the notional exceeds the clearing threshold.Vanilla FX Options (European-style calls and puts) for strategic hedging of the seasonal LatAm sales pipeline, purchased from a Tier-1 Spanish bank under the bank's appropriateness assessment; exotic, barrier or digital pay-off structures are rejected by Spanish treasury policy because they impair hedge-accounting clarity.FX Swaps with rollover (TOM/NEXT swap structures) for managing short-term liquidity mismatches between EUR receipts and USD/CNY supplier payments without changing the net open currency exposure.Liquidity-backed natural hedging and netting: the SL is permitted to denominate trade-enablement invoices with LatAm distributors in EUR where commercially viable, thereby eliminating the need for local-currency derivatives and reducing the hedge ratio to the residual net exposure; the treasury policy caps derivative-driven hedge ratios at 75% of projected net FX exposure so that all derivative use remains flow-hedging rather than speculative under AEAT and CNMV prudential expectations.

E-commerce / gateway settlement fit: Feasibility rating: MEDIUM for EU-licensed Electronic Money Institutions that hold a valid PSD2 passport into Spain; LOW for offshore or non-EU digital EMIs. A Spanish SL may lawfully hold payment accounts with an EU-authorised EMI, but an EMI is not a credit institution, is not supervised by the Banco de España as a bank, cannot grant overdraft or working-capital credit, cannot issue commercial documentary letters of credit or standby guarantees in the manner of a Tier-1 bank, and its deposit-like balances do not benefit from the Fondo de Garantía de Depósitos (Spanish deposit-guarantee scheme); immunity is replaced by the safeguarding/segregation duties of the EMD. Offshore EMIs (e.g., UK post-Brexit, BVI, UAE, Gibraltar-based) are not passportable into Spain without a local licence or authorised agent under the Payment Services Law (RDL 19/2018 transposing PSD2), so their onboarding of a Spanish manufacturing SL is either illegal or operationally crippled by correspondent-bank sanctions screening. For this micro-mobility OEM, which must pay Chinese component suppliers, collect LatAm distributor proceeds, settle Spanish payroll/VAT and ultimately remit dividends, an EMI-only treasury is not viable. The recommended configuration is a Tier-1 Spanish bank as the principal operating account and EBICS-connected gateway, optionally supplemented by one EU-passporting EMI multi-currency wallet for low-value, high-volume supplier float; any non-EU foreign account held by the SL must be disclosed to AEAT on Form 720 before 31 March of the following year, and balances above EUR 50,000 require the annual asset declaration, all of which raises compliance cost.

Statutory deliverableDeadline window Government feeDelinquency sanctions
Depósito de Cuentas Anuales (Annual Financial Statements Deposit): preparation, shareholders' meeting approval, and filing of the annual accounts, management report and, where applicable, statutory audit opinion with the Mercantile Registry Ordinary General Meeting must be held within six months of the fiscal year end (by June 30 for a January 1 – December 31 year-end); approved accounts must be deposited at the Mercantile Registry within one month after approval, i.e., no later than July 31 for a December 31 fiscal year end, under Articles 365 and 366 of the Ley de Sociedades de Capital $25 USD Closure of the company's registry sheet (cierre registral) after a formal warning annotation, blocking registration of successive corporate acts (capital increases, director appointments, share transfers) and preventing issuance of positive registry certificates; administrative fine from EUR 100 to EUR 12,000 under Article 378 of the Reglamento del Registro Mercantil (commonly 0.75‰ of total assets, minimum EUR 100)
Impuesto sobre Sociedades — Annual Corporate Income Tax Return (Modelo 200) for the Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada Within 25 calendar days following the six-month period after the fiscal year close, i.e., by July 25 for a December 31 fiscal year end, pursuant to Article 124 of Ley 27/2014 (Impuesto sobre Sociedades); payment accompanying the return is due on the same filing date $0 USD Late-filing surcharges (recargos) under Article 27 of Ley 58/2003 of 5% (within 3 months), 10% (3–6 months), 15% (6–12 months), or 20% (after 12 months, plus late-payment interest) of the self-assessed liability; Article 198 LGT fixed penalties from EUR 200 to EUR 20,000 proportioned to the unreported tax base; aggravated non-filing may trigger administrative collection proceedings, embargo of assets, and tax-lien registration
Legalización Electrónica de Libros — telematic legalization and stamping of statutory corporate and accounting books (Register of Members, Register of Directors, Minute Book, Inventory and Annual Accounts Book) at the Mercantile Registry Within the four months immediately following the date of approval of the annual accounts (Article 27.3 of the Código de Comercio); alternatively, before placing in service any newly opened statutory book $13 USD Unlegalized books lose privileged probative value in commercial disputes and courts may disregard them as evidence; the omission may be treated as a formal defect in the accounts deposit procedure and may expose the company to the Mercantile Registry nominal penalty scale (EUR 100 – EUR 1,000)
Annual return deadline

Ordinary General Meeting must be held within six months of the fiscal year end (by June 30 for a January 1 – December 31 year-end); approved accounts must be deposited at the Mercantile Registry within one month after approval, i.e., no later than July 31 for a December 31 fiscal year end, under Articles 365 and 366 of the Ley de Sociedades de Capital

Statutory government annual fee

$25 USD

Late filing penalties

Closure of the company's registry sheet (cierre registral) after a formal warning annotation, blocking registration of successive corporate acts (capital increases, director appointments, share transfers) and preventing issuance of positive registry certificates; administrative fine from EUR 100 to EUR 12,000 under Article 378 of the Reglamento del Registro Mercantil (commonly 0.75‰ of total assets, minimum EUR 100)

Strike-off trigger

Mandatory Audit Threshold Mandatory Audit for All Entities

Turnover: Mandatory independent audit under Article 263 of the Ley de Sociedades de Capital and Ley 22/2015 de Auditoría de Cuentas when the SL exceeds at least two of the following three thresholds at fiscal year close for two consecutive years: (i) total assets exceeding EUR 2,850,000; (ii) net annual turnover exceeding EUR 5,700,000; (iii) average workforce exceeding 50 employees. Mandatory audit also applies to parent companies preparing consolidated accounts, to entities qualifying as public-interest entities, and to companies whose shareholders holding at least 5% of share capital request a statutory audit under Article 265 LSC

Corporate Tax & Transfer Pricing

Corporate income tax (CIT), box-by-box return breakdown, dividend WHT, and director personal liability.

Statutory corporate income tax (CIT)

25%

Dividend withholding tax (WHT)

0% for dividends paid to Spanish resident companies; 19% for dividends paid to non-resident companies (reduced by applicable double tax treaties)

Mandatory Return Breakdown

Deadline: · Frequency:

25 days after the end of the tax period (for calendar year, by 25 January of the following year)

Box-by-Box Return Breakdown (non-resident focus)

BoxField Non-resident guidanceTax-evasion pitfall
Box 1 / Line 1a Taxable net income before tax deductions and exemptions N/A for resident Spanish entities; non-residents file Modelo 210 for Spanish source income Late filing: 100 euros per day (maximum 1,500 euros); additional 0.5% of the tax due per month of delay; criminal sanctions for willful non-compliance
Box 2 / Line 2a Taxable income after adjustments For non-residents, include Spanish source income subject to 19% WHT or treaty rates Late filing: 100 euros per day (maximum 1,500 euros); additional 0.5% of the tax due per month of delay; criminal sanctions for willful non-compliance

Transfer Pricing & Economic Substance

Master / Local File threshold: Mandatory Local File if annual consolidated revenue exceeds 20 million euros; Master File required if group consolidated revenue exceeds 50 million euros

Economic substance scope: Spain implements Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) pursuant to EU Directive 2018/410, requiring adequate substance for entities engaged in relevant activities such as holding intellectual property, financing, or distribution to avoid artificial tax avoidance

Fatal Compliance Red Lines & Director Liability

Tax Evasion

Statutory sanction: Criminal offense with fines up to 100% of evaded tax plus imprisonment from 6 months to 4 years

Director personal liability: Directors personally liable for restitution of evaded taxes, fines, and possible disqualification from company management; potential criminal prosecution
Transfer Pricing Non-Compliance

Statutory sanction: Administrative fines up to 5% of the adjusted taxable base; potential tax reassessment with interest and penalties

Director personal liability: Directors may face personal fines and disqualification if negligence or willful misconduct is proven
Shell Company / Lack of Economic Substance

Statutory sanction: Dissolution of company, back taxation, and fines up to 1 million euros; potential criminal liability under AML or tax avoidance rules

Director personal liability: Personal liability for fines, imprisonment for fraudulent bankruptcy or tax evasion, and entry bans
AML / Money Laundering Violations

Statutory sanction: Administrative sanctions up to 2 million euros or 10% of annual turnover; criminal penalties including fines and imprisonment

Director personal liability: Directors personally liable for fines, disqualification, and potential criminal charges
